sections.title: What makes a threat actor
content: Threat actor: any person or group that poses a threat
Four attributes: internal or external, funding, sophistication, motivation
Six actors to know: nation-state, organised crime, hacktivist, insider, unskilled attacker, shadow IT
examples: A disgruntled ex-employee and a government spy agency are both threat actors, but they score completely differently on all four attributes.
say: Today is objective 2.1, the people behind attacks. The exam rarely asks you to define an attacker; it describes one and expects you to recognise who it is.
The trick is to profile them with four questions. Are they inside or outside the organisation? How much money do they have? How skilled are they? And what do they want?
Learn the pattern of answers for each group and most questions in this area become straightforward.

checks.question: Name the four attributes you can use to describe any attacker.
checks.expect: Internal or external, resources or funding, sophistication or skill, and motivation.

sections.title: Nation-states and organised crime
content: Nation-state: government-backed, unlimited funding, very high skill
Nation-state goals: espionage and war. Months of hidden access
APT = advanced PERSISTENT threat. Long dwell time is the signature, usually a nation-state
Organised crime: external, well funded, high skill, money is the only goal
Ransomware run as a business
examples: SolarWinds, a nation-state campaign that sat hidden inside networks for months
REvil, a ransomware gang run like a company, with affiliates and profit shares
say: Both groups are outsiders with deep pockets and real skill, so the way to separate them is what they want. A government wants secrets or the ability to disrupt another country. A criminal gang wants to be paid.
The word persistent is the giveaway for an advanced persistent threat. If a question describes attackers quietly staying inside a network for months, think nation-state.
Pinning an attack on a particular group or country is rarely certain. Skilled groups reuse each other's tools and sometimes plant false clues to point investigators at someone else.

checks.question: Both a nation-state and an organised crime group are external, rich and skilled. What is the clearest way to tell them apart in a question?
checks.expect: Their motivation: nation-states want espionage or disruption, organised crime wants money.

checks.question: What does the word persistent tell you about an advanced persistent threat?
checks.expect: The attacker stays hidden inside the network for a long time, a long dwell time.

misconceptions.belief: Any attack that uses ransomware must be the work of organised crime.
misconceptions.correction: Ransomware is a strong hint of organised crime, but the tool alone does not prove who is behind it; look at the motive and the other clues.

sections.title: Hacktivists and unskilled attackers
content: Hacktivist: variable skill, ideological, acts for a CAUSE
Hacktivist methods: defacement, DDoS, leaks
Unskilled attacker (script kiddie): low skill, uses pre-built tools
Unskilled attacker motive: notoriety or curiosity. Still dangerous
examples: Anonymous defacing a government website to protest a policy
A teenager running a downloaded attack tool against a school network to see what happens
say: Hacktivists want attention for their beliefs, so their attacks are loud. Defacing a website, knocking it offline with a flood of traffic, or leaking embarrassing documents all send a public message.
An unskilled attacker borrows tools other people wrote. Do not dismiss them on the exam. Pre-built tools can be very powerful, and running them carelessly can still cause real damage.

checks.question: A group leaks a company's internal emails to embarrass it over its environmental record, and asks for nothing. Which kind of attacker does that suggest?
checks.expect: A hacktivist, because the motive is a cause or belief, not money.

misconceptions.belief: A script kiddie has no real skill, so they are not a genuine threat.
misconceptions.correction: Their skill is low but the tools they borrow are effective, so they can still cause serious harm.

sections.title: Insiders and shadow IT
content: Insider threat: has AUTHORISED access, so bypasses the perimeter
Insiders can be malicious or accidental. Motives: revenge or money
Shadow IT: unauthorised tools used for convenience
Shadow IT is internal, usually NOT malicious, but an unmanaged risk
examples: A sacked administrator deletes backups on their last day
A team shares client files through a personal cloud storage account because the approved system is slow
say: The insider is dangerous for one reason: they are already inside. Firewalls and perimeter defences are built to keep outsiders out, so they do little against someone with a valid login.
Not every insider means harm. Someone who clicks the wrong thing or emails the wrong file is still an insider threat.
Shadow IT is the odd one out on the list. Nobody is trying to attack anything; staff are simply getting work done with tools the security team cannot see or manage.

checks.question: Why can perimeter defences such as a firewall do so little against an insider?
checks.expect: The insider already has authorised access inside the network, so they never need to cross the perimeter.

checks.question: If shadow IT is not malicious, why is it still counted as a threat?
checks.expect: The tools are unmanaged and unknown to security, so data in them is unprotected and unmonitored.

sections.title: Matching motive to actor
content: Financial gain or blackmail: organised crime, malicious insiders
Espionage: nation-states, corporate competitors
War or disruption of infrastructure: nation-state
Philosophical or political beliefs: hacktivists
Revenge: disgruntled current or former employees. Ethical: researchers, bug bounty hunters. Notoriety: unskilled attackers
examples: A rival firm paying someone to copy a competitor's product designs is espionage, even though no government is involved
say: When a question gives you a motive, work backwards to the attacker. Money points to criminals or a greedy insider. Beliefs point to hacktivists. Shutting down a power grid points to a government.

Two motives catch people out. Espionage is not only for governments, because businesses spy on rivals too. And ethical hacking is a motive as well: researchers and bug bounty hunters break in to report flaws, not to exploit them.

checks.question: Which motive on the list belongs to people who are trying to help the organisation they attack?
checks.expect: Ethical, such as security researchers and bug bounty hunters.

misconceptions.belief: Espionage always means a foreign government is involved.
misconceptions.correction: Corporate competitors also carry out espionage to steal trade secrets.

sections.title: Profiling an attacker
content: Inside or outside?
Funding and skill: low, high or very high?
What do they want?
examples: Inside, low skill, no harm meant, convenience: shadow IT
say: Use the same four questions every time. Start with inside or outside, because that alone cuts the list roughly in half.
Then let the motive settle it. Skill and funding usually confirm the answer rather than decide it.

checks.question: An attacker is outside the company, has huge resources, and wants to disable a country's water treatment plants. Who is it most likely to be?
checks.expect: A nation-state, because the motive is disruption of infrastructure and the resources are very high.

application.scenario: A hospital finds three problems in one month. Attackers who had been hiding in the network for eight months were copying research data. A former IT contractor used an old account to wipe a server after being let go. Nurses were found sharing patient lists in a free messaging app because it was quicker than the official system.
application.question: Profile the attacker behind each of the three problems using the four attributes, and name each one.
application.expect: Long hidden access copying research: nation-state or APT, external, very high skill and funding, espionage. Wiped server: malicious insider, internal, revenge. Messaging app: shadow IT, internal, low skill, convenience, not malicious.

sections.title: The attribute matrix
content: Nation-state: external, VERY high funding and skill, espionage or war
Organised crime: external, high funding and skill, FINANCIAL
Hacktivist: external, low to mid funding, variable skill, IDEOLOGICAL
Insider: internal, low funding, low to mid skill, revenge or money
Unskilled attacker: external, very low everything, notoriety. Shadow IT: internal, low, convenience
examples: Long hidden presence = APT. Authorised access = insider. Unapproved app = shadow IT
say: Notice the pattern. Funding and skill are highest for nation-states and lowest for unskilled attackers and shadow IT, and only two of the six are internal.
The traps are usually the motives. Money means criminals or a greedy insider, a cause means hacktivists, and showing off means an unskilled attacker. Shadow IT is the one with no bad intent at all.

checks.question: Which two of the six attackers are internal, and which of those usually means no harm?
checks.expect: Insiders and shadow IT are internal; shadow IT is usually not malicious.

checks.question: A group wants to be noticed and boast online, but uses only tools it downloaded. Which attacker fits?
checks.expect: An unskilled attacker, sometimes called a script kiddie, motivated by notoriety.

retrieval.question: Think of a cyber attack you have heard about in the news. Who do you think was behind it, and what did they want?
retrieval.expect: Any reasonable example naming an attacker type and a motive, such as a ransomware gang wanting money.

retrieval.question: Why might an employee be just as dangerous to a company as an outside hacker?
retrieval.expect: They already have access inside, so they do not need to break through external defences.

exam_questions.q: Which actor is primarily motivated by financial gain?
exam_questions.why: Cybercriminals, such as organised crime groups running ransomware, attack for money. Hacktivists want a cause, nation-states want espionage or disruption, and researchers are ethical.

exam_questions.q: Which actor is associated with ideological or social causes?
exam_questions.why: Hacktivists act on political or philosophical beliefs, using defacement, DDoS and leaks to promote a cause.

options: Every actor uses the same tools
Techniques and infrastructure can overlap or be deliberately misleading
exam_questions.answer: Techniques and infrastructure can overlap or be deliberately misleading
exam_questions.why: Different groups reuse the same tools and servers, and skilled attackers can plant false clues, so evidence may point to the wrong group.

added_facts: Attribution is uncertain because groups reuse each other's tools and can plant false clues (needed for the pack's attribution exam question, which the notes do not cover).
REvil worked as ransomware-as-a-service with affiliates and profit shares (expanding the notes' 'ransomware as a business').
SolarWinds attackers stayed hidden for months (consistent with the notes' 'months of hidden access').
DDoS spoken as 'a flood of traffic knocking a site offline'.
Water treatment plants and power grids used as examples of infrastructure for the 'war or disruption' motive.
